blocks.text: Amorphous solids, contrary to crystalline solids, do not possess regular three-dimensional geometrical shapes. Examples are glass, wood, amorphous (plastic) sulfur, charcoal, coal and coke.

items: They can have small regions where the particles are orderly arranged, called crystallites, but they have no long-range regularity.
Amorphous solids such as glass melt over a wide range of temperature.
They can be moulded and blown into different shapes.
They have no definite value of heat of fusion.

blocks.prompt: Why can glass be blown into bottles while a crystal of sodium chloride cannot be shaped that way?
blocks.explanation: Glass is amorphous: it has no long-range order and no sharp melting point, so on heating it softens gradually over a range of temperature into a thick liquid that can be moulded and blown before it hardens. Sodium chloride is crystalline, with a sharp melting point; it stays rigid until it suddenly melts to a thin liquid, so there is no soft stage in which to shape it.

items: Amorphous solids (glass, wood, plastic sulfur, charcoal, coal, coke) have no regular shape, only small ordered crystallites, melt over a range, can be moulded and blown, and have no definite heat of fusion.
